SK2212 The loop body cannot run more than once

Every path through the loop body ends in a jump out of it, so the loop is an if that has been given the shape of a loop.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS1751

Why

A body that always breaks or returns consumes exactly one element and stops. Either the jump is in the wrong place — it belongs under a condition that is missing — or the loop is, and what was wanted is FirstOrDefault, a single if, or an index. The shape survives review because it reads as a loop and is one only in the grammar: the word foreach promises repetition the body has already ruled out. ⚠ The question is settled by control flow, not by looking at the last statement, and that is what makes it decidable rather than a heuristic. It is also what gets break right inside a nested switch, where the break binds to the switch and leaves the loop running — the reading a syntactic rule gets wrong, and the one this rule has a fixture for. There is no fix: which of the two readings was meant is exactly what the rule cannot know, and S1751 marks its own quick fix infeasible for the same reason.

Example

Instead of:

foreach (var item in items) {
    Handle(item);
    break;
}

Write:

foreach (var item in items) {
    Handle(item);
    if (Done(item)) { break; }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ A body whose endpoint is unreachable is not automatically a body that jumps out, and this is the rule's main guard. Control can fail to reach the end because every path jumps — the finding — or because a statement in the body never completes. A nested loop with a constant-true condition is the way that happens on purpose, so a body containing one is declined outright, as is a body containing any goto, whose cycles this analysis does not chase. ⚠ A jump the rule can point at is required, and the corpus is why. The first draft also reported a body with an unreachable endpoint and no exit point at all, reasoning that only an always-throw body could be left once the two guards above had run. Vixen's GlBindingPlan.Build refuted that: a switch expression over an error type — DescriptorKind was CS0246 in that compilation — makes the endpoint unreachable too, and the same shape with the enum resolved is correctly declined, measured on a probe that compiles. Requiring a return, a break or a goto that leaves the loop closes a class this rule cannot enumerate. The price is a body that throws on every path, which is a different finding from a loop that runs once. ⚠ A `continue` for this loop withdraws the finding. continue ends the iteration and not the loop, so a body ending in one has an unreachable endpoint and still runs to completion; the brief that produced this rule named it as the trap and there is a fixture for it. ⚠ A `break` belonging to a nested `switch`, or to a nested loop, does not count, because the exit points come from AnalyzeControlFlow over the body region and Roslyn binds those jumps to their own enclosing statement rather than to this loop. A break in a switch section whose loop therefore keeps running is a negative fixture. ⚠ A `return` or `throw` inside a lambda or a local function declared in the body belongs to that lambda, not to the loop, and the same region analysis excludes it. A loop with no body statements at all is not reported: there is no jump, and an empty loop is a different finding. Generated code is excluded.
